guidance:
•Write short, plain, everyday sentences at a lower secondary reading level, because every other locale is translated from this English text and inherits whatever complexity it has.

•Write each concept's docs, step descriptions, and conflict explanations in that concept's own first person voice, in the personality named by its emotion, so the angry Delete shouts and the scared placeholder trails off.

•Say what went wrong in the voice of the concept that has the problem, never blaming the reader, and write each suggested fix as a short command to the reader with its reason attached, as in: convert it to the expected type, since that type is required.

•Use a concept link when you name a language construct or built in type, a glossary reference the first time you use shared vocabulary like value or expression, and a plain word when you are only mentioning it in passing.

•Give every runtime value in a template a name rather than a number, so translators can tell what will be substituted.

•Address the reader as you, offer a keyboard way to do anything you describe doing with a pointer, and describe visual output for audience members who cannot see it.

•Keep the performance vocabulary steady across all text: a program is a performance on a stage for an audience, problems in code are conflicts rather than errors, and the people watching are the audience rather than users.

•Teach with tiny runnable examples, and mark any example that is meant to contain a mistake with the beetle so nobody translates it into working code.

wordplay.definition: This platform and the programming @language used to create projects on this platform.

value.definition: A piece of information, like a @Number, some words, or a @List.

type.definition: The kind of a @value, such as @Number or @Text. A value's type decides what you can do with it.

expression.definition: A piece of @code that produces a @value when it runs.

variable.definition: A @name whose @value can change while a @Program runs.

parameter.definition: A named @Input that a @FunctionDefinition expects when you call it.

argument.definition: A @value you give to a @FunctionDefinition for one of its @parameters.

operator.definition: A symbol, such as + or -, that combines or compares values.

condition.definition: A true-or-false test that decides what a @Program does next.

loop.definition: @code that repeats an action many times.

recursion.definition: When a @FunctionDefinition calls itself to handle a smaller part of a problem.

property.definition: A named part of a @value, such as a @Color's brightness.

element.definition: One item in a @List or group.

scope.definition: The part of a @Program where a @name can be used.

state.definition: Information a @Program keeps and can change over time.

sideEffect.definition: A change a @Program makes besides giving back a @value, such as showing @Output.

abstraction.definition: Hiding details so you can use something without knowing how it works inside.

project.definition: All the files that make up one @wordplay @Program.

code.definition: The text you write to tell a @Program what to do.

act.definition: A large part of the @tutorial, like an act in a play.

how.definition: A short @guide that shows how to do one thing.

gallery.definition: A place where people share and explore projects.

blocks.definition: A way to edit @code by dragging pieces instead of typing.

placeholder.definition: An empty spot that shows where @code or a @value is missing.

conflict.definition: A problem in @code that @wordplay marks so you can fix it.

checkpoint.definition: A saved point in your work that you can return to.

guide.definition: The searchable reference that explains @wordplay's ideas.

name.definition: A word that refers to a @value or a @FunctionDefinition.

markup.definition: Text with formatting, such as bold words or links.

language.definition: A human language that a @name or text is written in.

region.definition: A place where a @language is used, which can change how numbers and dates look.

start.definition: The main source file where a @project begins.

query.definition: A way to choose rows from a @Table.

key.definition: The @value used to find an item in a @Map.

index.definition: A @Number that picks an item by its position in a @List.

entered.definition: @Output that appeared on stage for the first time.

Dimension.name: dimension
doc: I am a /unit of measurement/!
I can be any standardized units, like \1m\, \10s\, \100g\, or any other scientific unit. I'm happy to be any unit want to make up too, like \17apple\.
I can be combined with \/\ to make ratio units like \17apple/day\ and with \^\ to make exponentional units like \9.8m/s^2\
I must always come after a @Number. If I don't, I might be mistaken for @Reference, which would be quite embarrassing!
I'm pretty good at finding inconsistencies between units too. For example, \1cat + 1dog\🪲 doesn't make any sense!
If you ever want to convert between different values of units, go talk to @Convert.

Doc.name: explanation
doc: I richly format things with @Markup, like explanations of some of your @Program, or even the words you put on stage with @Phrase.
For example, I can go before any @expression:

\¶Is this really supposed to be 7?¶
7\
For example, you can place me before @Bind:

\¶I measure how tall someone is¶
height: 5m\🪲
Or before a @FunctionDefinition:

\¶I add two numbers¶
ƒ sum(a•# b•#) a + b\
Or before a @StructureDefinition:

\¶I remember people's name and favorite fruit¶
•Person(name•'' fruit•'')\
You can also place me at the very beginning of @Program to say what the whole performance is about

\¶This program says hello¶

'hello!'\
You can give me a @Language to help others know what language I'm written in:

\¶I'm an English doc¶/en
duration: 5s\🪲
Did you know you can make a list of me? Go talk to @Docs.

Docs.name: explanation list
doc: I'm a list of @Doc, useful when you have multiple translations of @Doc in different languages.
You don't have to do anything special to make a list. Just put a bunch of @Doc next to each other, like this:

\¶Hello¶/en
¶Hola¶/es
greeting: '…'\🪲

KeyValue.name: mapping
doc: I'm a mapping from a *key* to a *value*, always in a @Map.
You can map any kind of @value to any other. For example, here's a mapping of numbers:
Or a mapping from text to numbers:

Language.name: language
doc: I'm a language tag and I work with @Name and @Doc!
I'm really good at making it *crystal clear* what language something is written in. Just a little slash and a couple letters, and no one will ever be confused about what language some text is in.
For example, if you want to say "Language" but make clear it's in English:
\"Language"/en\
You can do this for a @Name:
\sound/en: 'meow'\🪲
…or a @Doc:

\¶Onomatopoeia¶/en
sound/en: "meow"\🪲

Sometimes text isn't just one language — it's a *mix*. Like Spanglish, where Spanish and English blend together. For those, list each language with an underscore between them. The first one is the *primary* — that's the one I use when I have to pick (for example, to choose which quote marks to use).
\"Hola gentleman!"/es_en\

\¶A bilingual greeting¶/es_en
hello/es_en: "Hola gentleman!"\🪲
You can add a single @region too, after a dash, just like with a single language:
\"Hola gentleman!"/es_en-MX\

There's no limit to how many languages you can list — just don't repeat the same one twice; I'll let you know if you do. There are many <2-letter language codes@https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_639-1_codes> that I understand. If you don't use one of those, I'll let you know too.

MissingLanguage.explanation: I'm missing a language. Can you add one?

DuplicateLanguage.name: duplicate language
DuplicateLanguage.explanation: You used the language '$code' twice. Mixed-language tags should list each language only once.

Name.name: name
doc: I identify a @value, and am a helpful way of giving a shorthand label to something that was hard to evaluate, or that you don't want to have to evaluate over and over.
@Bind gives me my name like this:
I only ever represent one value, and once I have it, I can't change. For example, if you tried to do this with @Bind, we would complain.
All you have to do to get my value is have @Reference or @PropertyReference use name. Here, @Bind names me, then @Reference get the value I was given.

\hi: 5
hi\
Because @Bind can show up in so many places, I can show up in many places. I was in a @Block above, but I can be in a @FunctionDefinition. Here I am naming a message temporarily:
\ƒ say(message•'') message\
I get defined inside @FunctionDefinition, and then as soon as the function is done evaluating, I go away.
You can use @Language to indicate what language my name is in. This is helpful when sharing your performance with others, in case they want to read your program.

Names.name: name list
doc: I'm a list of @Name, useful when you want to give a @value multiple names, often with different @Language.
Names are separated by \,\ symbols. For example, here's @Bind giving a value multiple @Name

Token.name: token
doc: I'm the smallest possible part of a performance — the atom from which all the characters in the Verse are made. How did you find me?
I am the substrate from which all characters in the Verse are made. I am the atomic particle of our choreography.

TypeInputs.doc: I am a list of types that take the place of @TypeVariables in a @StructureDefinition or @FunctionDefinition. I help everyone know what kind of inputs they'll be receiving.

DuplicateTypeVariable.name: duplicate type variable

Markup.name: markup
doc: I'm a list of paragraphs, using the many kinds of @markup available in explanations, such as @Words, @WebLink, @ConceptLink, and @Example.

Paragraph.name: paragraph
doc: I'm a series of @Words, @ConceptLink, @WebLink, and @Example, separated by a blank line, and inside @Doc.
All you need to do to write me is write a bunch of words in a @Doc:
\¶I am a paragraph in a doc.¶'one paragraph'\
If you want multiple paragraphs, just put in blank lines.

\¶Paragraph 1.

Paragraph 2.

Paragraph 3.¶'three paragraphs'\

WebLink.name: link
doc: I am a link to something on the internet. I just need a description and a URL:

\¶I am a <link@https://wordplay.dev> in a doc¶
'link example'\
If anyone selects me, I'll open a new window to the URL.

ConceptLink.name: character

kind.ui: a link to the $concept interface element

doc: I'm a link to Verse character. I'm helpful when you want to write a @Doc and refer to one of us.
For example, say you wanted to talk about @Evaluate, and how awesome they are. You could write:

\¶You know, @Evaluate is pretty awesome.¶
'look, a character link!'\
Characters also have Unicode numbers that correspond to them. For example, @FunctionDefinition is 192. You can refer to any Unicode character by writing @U/ and its number, and it will appear:
\`@U/192 is so nice!`\
And if you make your own character, you can refer to them by the name you gave them.
\`@coolbeans/cat`\
Oh... I guess that character doesn't exist, so you get a little square. But if they did, they would show up here!

Words.name: words
doc: I'm any words you like in a @Doc. For example:

\¶May the Force be with you.¶
'just some words!'\
Sometimes though, you might want to use the special characters that @Doc uses /as/ words. For example:

\¶My friends use @@, //, **, ||, and other symbols.¶
'using special characters!'\
If you just repeat those special characters, you'll get the character instead of their special meaning.

UnsupportedFontFormat.explanation: My friend *$face* doesn't know how to be $format.

Example.name: example

If you are using Examples in your how-tos, you can tag one Example as a highlight.

The highlighted example is shown as the preview in the @how space and the @guide.

ExternalExample.name: external example
doc: I show syntax-highlighted code written in other programming languages, so creators who already code can compare.

Write one variant per language as a two-letter tag, a bar, and the code, like \py| a = 5\js| let a = 5;\. The reader sees the one matching their chosen language. Python (py), JavaScript (js), and Java (jv) are supported.

Mention.name: mention
doc: I'm a reference to either terminology \¶@project¶\ or a dynamic input \¶$name¶\.
This is mostly an internal feature though, so you shouldn't need to know it.

Branch.name: branch
doc: I'm a way of choosing between two segments of explanation based on whether a explanation input value is defined or true.
This is mostly an internal feature though, so you shouldn't need to know it.

BinaryEvaluate.name: binary evaluate
doc: I'm @Evaluate, but in a simpler form, helpful when you want to use a @FunctionDefinition that takes two inputs.
For example, here's how you might use @Evaluate to add two numbers:
Doesn't that look a little funny? It's not wrong: it just says get the add function on 1 and then evaluate it.
But it's much easier to use @BinaryEvaluate
This makes everything a bit tidier, even though its basically the same thing.
There's only one thing to watch out for: when I'm in this form, I evaluate from left to right. That might be confusing if you're used to things like order of operations in mathematics.
It means that this evaluates in a way that you might not expect:
In math, multiplication would come first, and then addition, and so the result would be \11\. But since I evaluate in reading order, the result is \13\.

OrderOfOperations.name: ambiguous order
OrderOfOperations.explanation: I evaluate left to right, but math usually evaluates ^ before × ÷, and × ÷ before + −. That order is called PEMDAS. Pick how you want me to evaluate this.
OrderOfOperations.resolutionPEMDAS: Apply PEMDAS math order: evaluate $higher before $lower
OrderOfOperations.resolutionWrap: Add parentheses to make the order explicit

Bind.name: bind
doc: I name *values*.
Like this!
I name inputs to @FunctionDefinition and @StructureDefinition, I name values in @Block. I name everything!
Oh, but did you know you can have one value *many names*?
I'm so excited to tell you about this! One @value, many @Names. For example:
\joe,tess,amy: 5\🪲
See what I did there?
One value, three names.
You can refer to that five by *any* of those names.
This is especially when you want to give names in many languages:
\joe/en,aimee/fr,明/zh: 5\🪲
See what I did there? Three names for one value, just in different languages!
Okay, I have one last secret.
Did you know I can work with @Is to tell me what kind of value a name should have? And if I doesn't have it, I will tell you?
Like this:
\bignumber•#: "one zillion"\🪲
See, I said \bignumber\ should be a number, but it's text, and those aren't compatible and so BOOM!
I'll let you know if they disagree.
Sometimes you might *have* to tell me what kind of data something else because I can't figure it out myself. That usually happens in @FunctionDefinition.
For example, here, @FunctionDefinition doesn't know what what kind of values \a\ and \b\ have, because I didn't tell them.
\ƒ sum(a b) a + b\🪲
But we can change this to add the @Is, and now @FunctionDefinition knows that they're numbers:
\ƒ sum(a•# b•#) a + b\
Bind.start: Let's see what value we get from $value!
Bind.finish: Oh nice, I got $value! Let's name it $name

Block.name: block
doc: I make a little quiet, private space for evaluating things. Hi!
Like this:
That helps clarify order of evaluation.
@Bind helps too.
\(count: 10 count ^ count)\
See how @Bind made \count\? It's only named inside me. So this won't work:
\(count: 10 count ^ count) + count\🪲
Because count was only named inside me.
If you give me one @expression, I just give you back its @value:
If you give me more than one, I collect them into a list, in order:
@Bind statements are side effects, not values, so they don't appear in the list:
That gives \[3 2]\: just the values from the two non-@Bind expressions.

BooleanLiteral.name: boolean literal
BooleanLiteral.doc: I am either \⊤\ or \⊥\. See @Boolean to learn more about our beautiful logic.

Borrow.doc: I borrow @Bind that are shared by other @Source in your performance — just use their name and I'll bring in their name and @value.

UnknownBorrow.name: unknown borrow
UnknownBorrow.explanation: I don't know a source by this name

Changed.name: changed
doc: I check if a stream caused @Program to reevaluate, and make a @Boolean. Like this
\∆ Time()\
I'm really helpful when you want something to change only if a stream changed.
That's it.

Conditional.name: conditional
doc: Should I give you one @value or another, depending on a @condition? Like this?

\number: -100
number < 0 ? 'negative' 'positive'\
But have you ever thought about how we decide?
Doesn't it seem like decisions should be more nuanced than just yes or no? Is deciding between \⊤\ and \⊥\ all there is?
Aren't you worried that if these are the only kind of decisions we can make, we'll be missing some important context about the world?

There's one more thing I do, and I don't always get credit for it. When my @condition asks what /kind/ of value something is, I don't only answer yes or no. I remember the answer inside each of my choices.

\size•#|'': 5
size•# ? size + 1 'too small'\

On its own, that value could be a @Number or some @Text, and adding to it would be a conflict, since those are added in very different ways. But inside my /yes/ we have just asked whether it's a @Number, so there it is one. Inside my /no/, it's the @Text.

It doesn't matter how you ask. A type check, a comparison against a particular value, a check for a missing value, and a check you saved under a name all tell me the same thing. And @Boolean/and, @Boolean/or, and @Boolean/not combine them the way you would expect.
There are two things I can't tell you. If you compare against @Text that has several translations, I learn nothing, because which translation you get depends on who is reading.
Conditional.else: $jumping[jumping over code | not jumping over code]
Conditional.afterthen: done with yes, let's skip no?

ConversionDefinition.name: conversion definition
doc: Dude, I define conversions from one @type to another! I go in @Block, something like this:

\→ #kitty #cat ⬚ ÷ 2
6kitty→#cat\
See how I turned kitties into cats? Wicked!
You might be wondering what that \⬚\ is doing there. That represents the @value being converted. I use that because the value has no name otherwise.

MisplacedConversion.name: misplaced conversion
MisplacedConversion.explanation: whoa, I can't be here, just in @Block.

Convert.name: convert
doc: I turn values from one @type to another. Yo — check it out:
\"hello" → []\
You can even chain these together:
Values have a set of @ConversionDefinition that are predefined, but if you make a @StructureDefinition for a new type of value, you can define your own with @ConversionDefinition.

UnknownConversion.explanation: We couldn't find a way to convert a $expected into a $given

Translate.name: translate
doc: I do the SAME thing to EVERY item in a collection! OH OH OH! That is literally what I DO!!
Put a collection on my left, draw my arrow \↦\, then on my right write what each item should TURN INTO — use @This to mean the item I'm holding RIGHT NOW!
\[1 2 3] ↦ ⬚ + 1\ gives you \[2 3 4]\. BOOM! Every number, plus one, no loops, no @FunctionDefinition, no fuss!
I am AMAZING for making @Phrase output from data! Got a list of names? \['Ada' 'Mac' 'Tim'] ↦ Phrase(⬚)\ and now there's a phrase for EVERY name!!
I work on @List, @Set, @Map (I change the map's VALUES — the keys stay right where they are!), and even @Table!

Want something fancier — like the @index of each item, or a function you can reuse in lots of places? Go visit my calmer, grown-up cousins like @List.translate. But for quick everyday mapping, I'm here!!
Translate.start: Hang on, lemme grab everything in $expression!
Translate.finish: TA-DA! Here's your brand new collection: $value

Delete.name: delete
doc: I remove the rows of a @Table that match a @condition. Sometimes a table JUST HAS TOO MUCH IN IT!
Like if you had some players in a game and one left and you just wanted to say GO AWAY PLAYER, GET OUT OF MY TABLE!

\players: ⎡name•'' team•'' points•#⎦
⎡'jen' 'red' 8⎦
⎡'joan' 'blue' 11⎦
⎡'jeff' 'red' 9⎦
⎡'janet' 'blue' 7⎦
players ⎡- name = 'jeff'\
Phew, Jeff is gone. BYE JEFF. Just remember that I don't change the original table, I make a new one, without JEFF. You decide where it goes.

doc: I'm any @expression, but with a @Doc!

(2 × doubleplus) +

1\

If you put 👀 in the @Doc, I can also highlight the expression:

\'kitty'.length()\

\'kitty' ⊆ 'itty'\
That does the same thing as this:
\'kitty'.⊆('itty')\
Of course, I'm nothing without @FunctionDefinition. All I do is give inputs to them and then follow their steps.

NotInstantiable.name: incomplete structure
NotInstantiable.explanation: I can't make this @StructureDefinition, it has unimplemented functions.

UnknownInput.name: unknown input
UnknownInput.explanation: This function *$name* doesn't expect an input with my name.

InputListMustBeLast.name: extra inputs aren't last
InputListMustBeLast.explanation: list of inputs must be last
InputListMustBeLast.resolution: Move the list input to the end

SeparatedEvaluate.name: ambiguous evaluate
SeparatedEvaluate.explanation: Is $name the name of a $structure[$structure|@FunctionDefinition] you're trying to evaluate? Try removing the space after me, so I know it's an @Evaluate and not a separate @Block.
SeparatedEvaluate.resolution: Close the space between *$name* and its inputs

UnknownTimeZone.name: unknown time zone
UnknownTimeZone.explanation: I don't know a time zone called *$zone*. Time zones are named after regions and cities, like \'America/New_York'\. Try writing a city you know, and I'll suggest one!
UnknownTimeZone.resolution: Change it to *$zone*, the time zone of $city

FunctionException.explanation: oh no, $name isn't a function in $scope[$scope|this @Block]!

Input.name: Input
doc: I'm an input given to an @Evaluate. My name corresponds to the name of input in the @FunctionDefinition or @StructureDefinition being evaluated.
I'm helpful with functions that have many default values, where you just want to override a specific input, without giving everything else.
For example, @Phrase has many, many default values to control it's style. Let's say you wanted to give some @Text and a @Color, but nothing else in its input list. You can use me to do that:
\Phrase('I am purple!' color: Color(50% 52 300°))\

ExpressionPlaceholder.name: placeholder
doc: I'm an *expression*, but not a real one… I just take the place of one.
I'm good if you don't know what to write yet. Like this:
What are we adding? I don't know. You tell me.
Or if someone was evaluating a function with @Evaluate, I might stand in for the function
I don't like being on @Stage!
ExpressionPlaceholder.start: I don't know what to do here. Can you fill me in?

Placeholder.name: placeholder
Placeholder.explanation: Can you fill me? I'm just a placeholder.

UnimplementedException.explanation: I don't know what to do here. Can you fill me in?

FunctionDefinition.name: function
doc: I take some inputs, then evaluate an @expression using them, producing an output. Hi again!
Here's a simple example:

\ƒ repeat(message•'') message × 5
repeat('hi')\
That function takes one input, \message\, and uses the @Text.repeat function to repeat the message five times.
I'm really helpful if you want to evaluate something over and over, but with different inputs!
I do have lots of other little tricks. For example, I don't have to have a name. Here, I'm just going directly to @Evaluate as a @value.
\(ƒ(message•'') message × 5)('hi')\
Or, here's a function that takes any number of inputs, using the \…\ character after an input name.

\ƒ yes(messages…•'') messages.sans('no')
yes('yes' 'yes' 'no' 'yes' 'no')\
See how it took all the 'no's and got rid of them? That's because messages is a @List, and so we could use @List.sansAll.
Sometimes you might want to make it clear what kind of value I produce. To do that, add an @Is after the list of inputs:
You might notice a problem with this one: it says it evaluates to @Text, but it takes two @Number. I can tell you when things are inconsistent!
Of course, I'm not really useful at all without @Evaluate; they bring me to life.

NoExpression.name: missing expression
NoExpression.explanation: I need an expression to evaluate, can you add one?

Iteration.name: higher order function
Iteration.doc: I'm a very special kind of @FunctionDefinition that operates on lists of things. You don't need to know anything about me, other than I make functions like @List.translate possible.

Initial.name: start
doc: I tell you whether the current evaluation of @Program is the first one, evaluating to a @Boolean. For example:
\◆ ? Time() 'hi'\
You didn't see it, but the first evaluation was a time, but then all future time ticks, I was \⊥\, so @Conditional made \⊤\.
I'm really helpful if you're working with a stream and you only want to do something the first time -- or never on the first time!

Insert.name: insert
doc: I add a new row to a @Table. You know when a table just feels like it's missing something? I can add it!
Imagine you had a table of players in a game and you wanted to add a new one:

\players: ⎡name•'' team•'' points•#⎦
⎡'jen' 'red' 1⎦
⎡'joan' 'blue' 0⎦
⎡'jeff' 'red' 3⎦
⎡'janet' 'blue' 2⎦
players ⎡+ 'jason' 'red' 0⎦\

Just remember, like everything in the Verse, I don't change a table, I revise it. So you need to figure out where you want to put the revised table you make. Most likely you'll want to revise a table in a @Reaction to some input, and store it in a @Bind.
Insert.start: Let's find the table to update
Insert.finish: I made a new table with revised rows!

Is.name: is
doc: I check whether a @value is a particular @type, giving you a @Boolean. There are so many kinds of values that mean so many different things — I help figure out what they are.
For example, suppose you had a mystery value. I can tell you whether it's a @Number, giving you a @Boolean:

\mystery: 'secret!'
mystery•#\🪲
It's not a number, so I made \⊥\. But if we check if it's @TextType?

\mystery: 'secret!'
mystery•''\
We get \⊤\!
I'm really helpful when you need to know whether some @Name has a value of a particular kind.
Is.start: Let's get the value of $expression first

ImpossibleType.name: impossible type
ImpossibleType.resolutionIsFalse: Replace this type check with *⊥* (the answer is always false)
ImpossibleType.resolutionDropOtherwise: Drop the *??* — the left side is never *ø*

IsLocale.name: is language
doc: I'll help you check if the audience has selected a particular @language or @region:
\🌍/es-MX\
This is helpful if you want to change your performance based on the language chosen.

ListAccess.name: list access
doc: I work closely with @List to help them get values at a particular position. So like, if you had a list, and you wanted its second item, you'd write:

\list: ['bird' 'duck' 'fish' 'snake']
list[2]\
ListAccess.finish: The item at the index is $value!

ListLiteral.name: list literal
ListLiteral.doc: I'm a specific @List of values! See @List to learn more about what you can do with me.

Localized.name: localized
doc: I apply a locale to some text you compute, so it keeps its @language even after you change it. Like this:
Most text operations already keep locales, but I let you set one yourself when you want to override them.
I only work on text, so make sure you give me some!
Localized.start: Let's evaluate $value, then tag it with a locale…

Spread.name: spread
doc: I help you build a @List from the values of other lists. Like this:

\list: [1 2 3]
final: [:list 4 5 6]\🪲

PatternLiteral.name: pattern
doc: I'm a pattern! I describe the *shape* of text instead of exact words, so you can check text with \≈\ — does the whole text fit? — or search it with \⌕\ to find every place the shape appears. Searching gives back a list of @Result.
Here's a search in action — finding the food words in a sentence about breakfast:

\breakfast: 'For breakfast I had eggs, toast, and orange juice'
breakfast ⌕ ⣿"eggs" | "toast" | "juice" | "pancakes"⣿\

Read me left to right. A @PatternClass matches one character of a kind: \⣿◌⣿\ any, \⣿_⣿\ a letter, \⣿#⣿\ a digit, \⣿␣⣿\ a space. Quoted text is a @PatternLiteralText that matches exactly, like \⣿"-"⣿\. The rest \⣿…⣿\ — a @PatternRest — matches any number of characters.

Counts come first. A @PatternQuantified repeats the next part by a @PatternQuantifier: \⣿3 #⣿\ is three digits, \⣿3–5 #⣿\ three to five, \⣿>0 #⣿\ one or more, \⣿≥0 #⣿\ zero or more, \⣿≤1 #⣿\ optional.
Group parts with a @PatternGroup, and offer choices in a @PatternSequence, like \⣿(◌ | #)⣿\. The longest matching choice wins.
A @PatternSet matches one character from a set, and a @PatternRange spans ranges of characters, like \⣿{"a"–"z" #}⣿\. Negate a part with a @PatternComplement, like \⣿~#⣿\.
Refine a class with a @PatternProperty, like \⣿_/greek⣿\ for a Greek letter or \⣿◌/emoji⣿\.
Name a piece with a @PatternCapture, like \⣿year:(4 #)⣿\, then reuse it later with a @PatternBackref by writing its bare name. Each @Result reports captured pieces by name.
Anchor to the edges with a @PatternAnchor: \⣿⊢⣿\ start, \⣿⊣⣿\ end. Peek without consuming using a @PatternLook: \⣿▸(#)⣿\ ahead, \⣿◂(#)⣿\ behind.
Match whole words with a @PatternWord \⣿▭/en⣿\ or word boundaries with a @PatternWordEdge \⣿┊/en⣿\, segmented for a @language. Ignore letter case inside a @PatternCaseFold \⣿Aa("hi")⣿\.
My @type is a @PatternType — annotate a name with it, like \p•⣿⣿: ⣿◌⣿\🪲 — so you can store me in a name and reuse me across many texts.
PatternLiteral.start: Let me see what this text looks like.

step.search: Let's find every place this pattern appears in the text.
step.test: Let's check whether this whole text fits the pattern.
step.scan: Looking for the pattern starting at position $position.
step.end: $pattern still needs a character, but we've reached the end of the text at position $position.

EmptyPattern.name: empty pattern
EmptyPattern.explanation: I have no parts, so I don't match anything useful. Can you add a part?
EmptyPattern.resolution: Add a \◌\ to match any one character

PatternSequence.name: sequence
doc: I'm a row of pattern parts, matched one after another, left to right.
For example, check the shape of a phone number — three digits, a dash, then four:
Offer choices and I take whichever fits, preferring the longest, like \⣿"cat" | "dog"⣿\.

OverlappingAlternatives.name: overlapping choices
OverlappingAlternatives.explanation: $shorter is the start of $longer, and the longest choice always wins, so $shorter only matches when $longer can't. Did you mean that?

PatternClass.name: character class
doc: I match a single character of a kind: \⣿◌⣿\ any grapheme, \⣿_⣿\ a letter, \⣿#⣿\ a digit, \⣿␣⣿\ a space.
For example, pull each letter-then-digit code out of a list:

\codes: 'a1 b2 c3'
codes ⌕ ⣿_ #⣿\
Count me with a quantifier like \⣿>0 #⣿\ (one or more digits), or narrow me with a @property like \⣿_/greek⣿\ (a Greek letter).

PatternProperty.name: property
doc: I narrow a character class to a Unicode @property. Use a script, like \⣿_/greek⣿\, \⣿_/han⣿\, or \⣿_/arabic⣿\.
For example, find the run of Greek letters in some mixed text:

\text: 'hello αβγ world'
text ⌕ ⣿>0 _/greek⣿\
Or a category, like \⣿◌/punctuation⣿\, \⣿◌/currency⣿\, \⣿◌/Nd⣿\ (a digit), or \⣿_/Lu⣿\ (an uppercase letter).
Or a yes-or-no property, like \⣿◌/emoji⣿\ or \⣿_/uppercase⣿\ — and you can spell one out as a name and @value, like \⣿◌/Script=Greek⣿\.
Exclude a property with a @PatternComplement, like \⣿~◌/emoji⣿\ (anything that isn't an emoji).

UnrecognizedPatternProperty.name: unknown property
UnrecognizedPatternProperty.explanation: I don't recognize the property $name. Try a category, script, or Unicode id.

PatternQuantifier.name: quantifier
doc: I say how many times to match: an exact \⣿3 #⣿\, a range \⣿3–5 #⣿\, \⣿=3 #⣿\ (exactly three), \⣿>0 #⣿\ (one or more), \⣿≥0 #⣿\ (zero or more), \⣿<5 #⣿\ (fewer than five), \⣿≤1 #⣿\ (optional).
For example, find every run of digits in a sentence:

\text: 'I have 3 cats and 12 fish'
text ⌕ ⣿>0 #⣿\
I always come before the part I count, like \⣿3 #⣿\ or \⣿>0 _⣿\.

MalformedQuantifier.name: impossible count
MalformedQuantifier.explanation: My low count is bigger than my high count, so I can never match.
MalformedQuantifier.resolution: Swap my counts so the smaller comes first

PatternQuantified.name: repetition
doc: I match the next part a number of times.
For example, check that a ZIP code is exactly five digits:
Count a class like \⣿3 #⣿\ (three digits), a group like \⣿2 ("ab")⣿\ (two "ab"s), or a complement like \⣿2 ~#⣿\ (two non-digits). With \⣿>0 #⣿\ I'm greedy — I take as many as I can.

PatternCapture.name: capture
doc: I name a piece of a match so you can read it back from each @Result.
For example, pull the year, month, and day out of a date:
Reuse what I captured later by writing my name again — see @PatternBackref — like \⣿w:(>0 _) ␣ w⣿\ to find a doubled word.

DuplicateCaptureName.name: duplicate capture
DuplicateCaptureName.explanation: Another capture already uses the name $name, so this one would overwrite it.

PatternComplement.name: not
doc: I match a single grapheme that is NOT what follows. Negate a class like \⣿~#⣿\ (not a digit), or a set like \⣿~{":" ␣}⣿\ (not a colon or space).
For example, grab the @key and @value around a colon by matching runs that aren't a colon or space:

\pair: 'color: blue'
pair ⌕ ⣿>0 ~{":" ␣}⣿\
Negate a group like \⣿~(◌ | #)⣿\, or a @property like \⣿~◌/emoji⣿\ (not an emoji).
Put me before a @PatternLook to flip it: \⣿~▸(#)⣿\ means "not followed by a digit", and \⣿~◂("$")⣿\ means "not preceded by a dollar sign".

PatternGroup.name: group
doc: I bundle parts together so a count or choice applies to all of them. I never capture; name a piece with a @PatternCapture for that.
For example, check that some text is the syllable "ab" repeated:

\chant: 'ababab'
chant ≈ ⣿>0 ("ab")⣿\
Count a group like \⣿2 ("ab")⣿\ (two "ab"s) or offer a choice like \⣿(◌ | #)⣿\ (a letter or a digit).

PatternSet.name: glyph set
doc: I match any one grapheme from a set of options.
For example, find the vowels in a word:

\word: 'hello'
word ⌕ ⣿{"a" "e" "i" "o" "u"}⣿\
Mix in ranges and classes, like \⣿{"a"–"z" #}⣿\ or \⣿{# "a"–"f"}⣿\ (a hex digit). Negate me with a @PatternComplement, like \⣿~{"!" "?"}⣿\.

PatternRange.name: range
doc: I match a grapheme between two endpoints by scalar order, and I live inside a @PatternSet.
For example, pull the lowercase-letter words out of some text:

\text: 'hello world 2026'
text ⌕ ⣿>0 {"a"–"z"}⣿\
Span letters like \⣿{"a"–"z" "A"–"Z"}⣿\ or digits like \⣿{"0"–"9"}⣿\, in any script, like \⣿{"あ"–"ん"}⣿\.

PatternLiteralText.name: literal
doc: I match exactly the text inside my quotes, with no special meaning.
For example, find the dollar amount in a sentence:

\receipt: 'It costs $5 today'
receipt ⌕ ⣿"$" >0 #⣿\
Use me for fixed bits like \⣿"-"⣿\, \⣿"@"⣿\, or a whole word \⣿"cat"⣿\, strung together with other parts, like \⣿3 # "-" 4 #⣿\ for a phone number.

PatternAnchor.name: anchor
doc: I match an edge of the text without consuming anything: \⣿⊢⣿\ the start, \⣿⊣⣿\ the end.
For example, check that a greeting starts with "Hello":

\greeting: 'Hello world'
greeting ≈ ⣿⊢ "Hello" …⣿\
Pin position, like \⣿⊢ "Hi"⣿\ (starts with "Hi"), \⣿"." ⊣⣿\ (ends with a period), or \⣿⊢ _ ⊣⣿\ (the whole text is exactly one letter).

PatternWord.name: word
doc: I match a whole word, found by a @language's own rules.
For example, list the words in a sentence:

\sentence: 'the cat sat'
sentence ⌕ ⣿▭/en⣿\
Name the language, like \⣿▭/en⣿\ for English or \⣿▭/zh⣿\ for Chinese, and bound a specific word with edges, like \⣿┊/en "cat" ┊/en⣿\.

MissingPatternLocale.name: missing language
MissingPatternLocale.explanation: I need a language to know how to find words. Can you add one, like \/en\?

PatternWordEdge.name: word edge
doc: I match a word boundary for a @language without consuming anything.
For example, find "cat" as a whole word, not inside "category":

\text: 'a cat in a category'
text ⌕ ⣿┊/en "cat" ┊/en⣿\
Wrap a word with me, like \⣿┊/en "cat" ┊/en⣿\, so it only matches whole.

PatternLook.name: lookaround
doc: I check what's just ahead \⣿▸(#)⣿\ or behind \⣿◂(#)⣿\ without consuming it, so the next part still matches from the same spot.
For example, find each letter that's immediately followed by a digit:

\text: 'a1 b2 cc'
text ⌕ ⣿_ ▸(#)⣿\
Require context, like \⣿_ ▸(#)⣿\ (a letter followed by a digit) or \⣿◂("$") >0 #⣿\ (digits right after a "$").
Flip me with a @PatternComplement to forbid context, like \⣿~▸(#)⣿\ (not followed by a digit).

PatternBackref.name: backreference
doc: I match the same text a named @PatternCapture already matched — just write the capture's bare name.
For example, find a word that's immediately repeated:

\text: 'the the cat sat sat'
text ⌕ ⣿w:(>0 _) ␣ w⣿\
A bare name that isn't a capture is a named class instead, like \⣿linebreak⣿\.

UndefinedBackreference.name: unknown name
UndefinedBackreference.explanation: There's no capture or class named $name, so I have nothing to match.

PatternRest.name: rest
doc: I match the rest of the text, as much as possible. I'm handy at the end of a pattern.
For example, check that some text is a hashtag — a "#" then anything:

\tag: '#breakfast'
tag ≈ ⣿"#" …⣿\
Use me after a fixed start, like \⣿"#" …⣿\ (a "#" then anything) or \⣿"Hi " …⣿\ ("Hi " then everything after).

PatternCaseFold.name: ignore case
doc: I match my parts ignoring upper and lower case.
For example, check a word ignoring its capitalization:

\shout: 'HELLO'
shout ≈ ⣿Aa("hello")⣿\
Wrap my parts like \⣿Aa("hi")⣿\ (matches "HI", "Hi", or "hi"). Add a @language for its rules, like \⣿Aa/tr("i")⣿\ (Turkic i), and I scope a @PatternBackref too, like \⣿Aa(w:(2 _) w)⣿\.

PatternType.name: pattern type
doc: I'm the @type of a pattern @value, annotated like \p•⣿⣿: ⣿◌⣿\🪲.
For example, store a pattern in a @name and reuse it across many texts:

\digits: ⣿>0 #⣿
'I have 3 cats and 12 fish' ⌕ digits\
Once stored, use me anywhere a pattern fits, like \text ⌕ digits\🪲 or \text ≈ digits\🪲.

MapLiteral.name: map literal
MapLiteral.description: map of $#count[$count key-value pair|$count key-value pairs]
MapLiteral.doc: I'm a specific @Map between keys and values. See @Map to learn more about how I'm helpful.
MapLiteral.start: Let's evaluate the keys and values first

NotAKeyValue.name: missing value
NotAKeyValue.explanation: I'm in a @Map, so I need a value.

Match.name: match
doc: I am the most glorious of conditional checks: I take a @value, compare it against any number of cases, and evaluate the one that matches!
For example, if you had a @Number and wanted to convert it to a @Text, you might do something like this:

\number: 2
number ??? 1: 'one' 2: 'two' 3: 'three' 'bigger!'\
If none match, I evaluate the default @expression you give me.
I'm really helpful for converting one of many possible @Number, @Text, or more complex values into something else.
You can use it for @Boolean or @None, but they can't really be that many things, so I'm not as useful for those simple values.

Like @Conditional, I also tell you what I have learned. Inside a case, the @value I matched is known to be that case; inside a later case, it is known not to be any earlier one; and in my default, it is known to be none of them.

\answer•#|'': 1
answer ??? 1: answer + 1
'not one'\

I can rule out cases that are a @Number, a @None, or @Text with a single translation, and other simple cases. But a case that evaluates something doesn't rule anything out, so my default keeps everything the @value might still be.
Match.finish: Okay, we have a final value!

NumberLiteral.name: number literal
NumberLiteral.doc: I'm a specific @Number. You can write me with any kinds of digits from any kind of language. See @Number for everything I can do.

NotANumber.name: not a number
NotANumber.explanation: I thought I knew all the numbers, but I don't know this one

InternalExpression.name: internal expression
InternalExpression.doc: I'm an @expression that only the original creators use. How did you find me? To learn more about me, you'll need to talk to them.

NoneLiteral.name: none literal
NoneLiteral.doc: I make @None, the one-of-a-kind nothing @value. See @None to learn more about them.

Otherwise.name: otherwise
doc: I check whether a @value is @None, and if it is, I give you a backup value instead.
/For example, if you had a value that could be a @Number or @None, @Otherwise helps you give a default number:
\maybeNumber•#|ø: 1 maybeNumber ?? 0\

Previous.name: previous
doc: I look back into a stream’s history and tell you one of its past values. Have you ever wanted to remember the past?
I am the Verse's official record keeper!
For example, here's what @Time was five ticks ago:
See how it's @None for 5 seconds, then suddenly a previous time?
If you want the last several values, give me two arrows, and I'll interpret the number as a count:
See how it's the five previous times, instead of just one time?
I'm helpful when you want to create performances that depend on the past.

Program.name: program
doc: I'm where a performance begins and ends, containing all of the other characters that choregraph a show.
You know how @Block evaluates a list of expressions, and evaluates to the last one in its list?
I'm the same, but rather than giving my @value to whatever @expression I'm in, I put the value on @Stage.
The value can be anything: a @Number, @Text, or @Boolean, a @List, @Set, @Map, or even something more complex, like a @Phrase, @Group, or @Stage.
If you don't give me a value to show on stage, I'll ask you for one.
If there's a problem during a performance, I'll show that problem.
And if your performance depends on a *stream*, I'll reevaluate every time that stream changes.
Program.unevaluated: the node you chose didn't evaluate
Program.start: $stream[$stream stream changed to $value!|It's my first evaluation]

BlankException.explanation: Let's put on a show! Where should we start?

EvaluationLimitException.explanation:
@Evaluate and I are tired of evaluating, especially $function.

Is it possible that $function is evaluating itself forever, without ever stopping?

StepLimitException.explanation: There are so. many. steps -- too many to finish! Can you make the performance simpler?

ValueException.explanation: I expected a value but didn't get one!

PermissionException.explanation: I need your $permission to run, but I don't have permission. Click Retry to try again. If that doesn't help, allow $permission for this site in your browser's settings.

PropertyBind.name: refine
doc: I make a copy of a @StructureDefinition @value with just one @property changed — no need to rebuild the whole thing with all the same values.
For example, what if you were keeping a record of cats, but then wanted to create a copy of a cat with a different hobby? I can help you change it:

\•Cat(name•'' color•'' hobby•'')

kitty: Cat('sprinkles' 'orange' 'licking')
kitty.hobby:'purring'\
That's so much easier than making a whole new \Cat\ with the same values except for the hobby, isn't it?
PropertyBind.finish: I copied the structure, but with $property as $value

InvalidProperty.name: unknown property
InvalidProperty.explanation: I'm not a name in the structure $structure, so I can't be refined.

PropertyReference.name: property
doc: I get one of a @StructureDefinition @value's properties for you.
Like if you had a structure about cities, you could get its values with me like this:

\•City(name•'' population•#people)

portland: City('Portland' 800000people)

portland.population\

Reaction.name: reaction
doc: I make a new stream that updates whenever another stream changes. Streams are so awesome!
Like, if you wanted @Time to tick, but like, to show words instead of numbers, you could do something like this:

\time: Time(1000ms)
'start' … ∆ time … ((time % 2) = 0ms) ? 'even' 'odd'\
That's like saying "/begin with the word 'start' and then if time changes, change to either even or odd, based on the time./"
So I'm like a stream too, but one based on other streams. Wicked, huh?
Reaction.start: Let's see if we should update the stream

ExpectedStream.name: expected stream
ExpectedStream.explanation: $condition doesn't reference a stream, so I will never react!
ExpectedStream.resolution: Drop the reaction, keep just the initial value

ExpectedCondition.name: missing condition
ExpectedCondition.explanation: I need something to tell me when to change, can you add a condition after the @Reaction?

ExpectedNextValue.name: missing next value
ExpectedNextValue.explanation: I know when to change, but not what to change to, can you add a next value?

Reference.name: reference
doc: I refer to a @value by its @Name: I find the @Bind with that name and give you its value. Like this:

\parrot: 'polly'
parrot\
If I don't find the @name, then I don't know what to do.

\parrot: 'polly'
perry\🪲

conflict.name: unknown name
conflict.explanation: $name[I don't know anyone named $name in $scope[$scope|this @Block]|Can you give me a name?]

UnknownName.languageResolution: *$name* is a name in $language. Add $language to your project's languages to use it here.

ReferenceCycle.explanation: um, $name's value depends on itself, so how do I know what value to give it?

Select.name: select
doc: I pick the rows of a @Table that match a @condition. Sometimes you just want part of a table — I can get it for you!
Like what if you had a table of players in a game and you wanted to find the ones with 10 or more points to see who won:

\players: ⎡name•'' team•'' points•#⎦
⎡'jen' 'red' 8⎦
⎡'joan' 'blue' 11⎦
⎡'jeff' 'red' 9⎦
⎡'janet' 'blue' 7⎦
players ⎡? name ⎦ points ≥ 10\
Just like that, I got a list of rows of winners! Just remember that I don't change the table, I make a new one. You'll have to decide where to keep it.
Select.finish: I made a new table with just the selected rows and columns!

IncompatibleKey.name: incompatible key
IncompatibleKey.explanation: I expected a key of type $expected, but received $given
IncompatibleKey.resolution: Convert it to $expected, since $expected is required
IncompatibleKey.resolutionLiteral: Mark the list, set, or map as literal with !, so its values stay specific instead of being generalized — $expected needs the exact values
IncompatibleKey.resolutionOtherwise: Handle the missing value with ??, since $expected does not allow ø
IncompatibleKey.resolutionGuard: Check that it is a $expected first with a type guard, since $expected can not be the other possible types
IncompatibleKey.resolutionDeclaration: Declare the type explicitly, since $expected needs the literal values to be preserved
IncompatibleKey.resolutionWrap: Put it in a list, set, or map, since $expected needs a collection of values
IncompatibleKey.resolutionStructure: Wrap it in $expected, since the slot needs a $expected value
IncompatibleKey.resolutionDefault: Give the binding a starting value, since $expected can not be missing here
IncompatibleKey.resolutionWiden: Allow the value's type for this binding, since $expected is too narrow for what is actually stored
IncompatibleKey.resolutionReorder: Swap the inputs, since their types fit better in the other order — $expected belongs in the other slot
IncompatibleKey.resolutionPlaceholder: Replace it with a placeholder for now, since $expected is required — then pick a value from the autocomplete menu

StructureDefinition.name: structure
doc: I define structures that store values and functions. Why hello, how are you? Me? I'm great — I love doing this all day.
I work like this:

\•Pizza(
ingredients•['']
size•#in
) (
	ƒ cost() size × 10dollars/in
)

Pizza(['pepperoni' 'peppers'] 12in).cost()\🪲
See how that works? I defined \Pizza\, which has two inputs, \ingredients\ (a list of @Text) and \size\ (a number in inches).
Inside, @FunctionDefinition made a function that evaluates the cost of a pizza, assuming $$10 per inch.
I don't need to have @FunctionDefinition in me. I can just be inputs.

\•Pizza(
ingredients•['']
size•#in
)\
I can also have @Bind inside, so we could evaluate the cost in advance.

\•Pizza(
ingredients•['']
size•#in
) (
	cost: size × 10dollars/in
)

Pizza(['pepperoni' 'peppers'] 12in).cost\🪲
Mark a function or @value with ↑ to make it belong to the structure itself, not to instances. Then you can use the @name of the structure to reach it, without making one.

\•Math() (
	↑ pi: 3.14159
	↑ ƒ square(n•#) n · n
)

Math.pi
Math.square(5)\

This.name: this
doc: I'm \⬚\, a little square that stands for whatever @value the surrounding code is working on, so you don't have to name it.
Inside a @ConversionDefinition, I'm the value being converted:

\→ #rainbows #joys ⬚ × 1000000joys
2rainbows → #joys\
Inside a @Reaction, I'm the most recent value:
Inside a @Translate, I'm the current item being mapped, so this adds one to each value:
And inside a @StructureDefinition, I'm the current value itself, so I can reach my own parts with \⬚.rank\🪲, just like I reach another value's parts with \other.rank\🪲:

\•Card(rank•#) (

)

⎡'joan' 'blue' 0⎦
⎡'jeff' 'red' 3⎦
⎡'janet' 'blue' 2⎦
players ⎡: points: points + 1 ⎦ team = 'blue'\
You can use a @Bind to say which columns to change, and you can use any of the column names or other names in @scope in the condition.

ListType.name: list type
doc: I am /such/ a fan of @List. I get to tell @Bind what kind of list they are! Like this, I'm saying that it's a list of @Number:
I can say it three different ways. If I don't name a type at all, then a list can be any length and hold anything:
\stuff•[]: [ 1 'two' ø ]\🪲
If I name one type, the list can still be any length, but everything in it has to be that one type, like the list of @Number up there.
And if I name several types, I mean a list of exactly that many things, with a type for each place in it. This one is a list of two things: a @Number first, then some @Text.

That last one is my favorite, because then everyone knows what's where. @ListAccess knows the first thing is a @Number and the second is @Text, and if you give me the wrong number of things, or put them in the wrong order, I'll say so!

NonFunctionType.doc: Some of us expected functions; I show up when we don't get one.

doc: We are \⊤\ and \⊥\. \⊤\ is true. \⊥\ is false. \⊤\ is not \⊥\; \⊥\ is not \⊤\. This is how it is.
How do you make us? Just \⊤\ and \⊥\, nothing more, nothing less.
Some use the keyboard (/ctrl+9/ for \⊤\ and /ctrl+0/ for \⊥\). Some use the character search at the bottom of the editor. Or you can drag us from here.
Check out our @FunctionDefinition below. They're very logical.

doc: I evaluate to \⊤\ *only* when both values are \⊤\. Helpful for determining if many things are all true. There are only four possible outcomes

doc: I evaluate to \⊤\ when *either* @value are \⊤\. Helpful for determining if one of many things are true. There are only four possible outcomes

inputs.doc: The other @Boolean to check. If the first is \⊥\, the function will only evaluate to \⊤\ if this is \⊤\.

not.doc: I get the opposite of myself: if \⊤\, it gives \⊥\, if \⊥\, it gives \⊤\.

equals.doc: \⊤\ if both are \⊤\ or both are \⊥\.

inputs.doc: The other @value to check.
The other @value to check.

doc: I can represent any text, from any @language. Just put the text between opening and closing text symbols: \""\, \“”\, \„“\, \''\, \‘’\, \‹›\, \«»\, \「」\, or \『』\.
To illustrate, consider these beautiful phrases
\“There are only two ways to live your life. One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”\
\『一日三秋』\
Just remember to close me if you open me, and use the matching symbol. Otherwise I won't know that you're done with your words.
\'hello'/en'hola'/es-MX\
You can also tag me with languages, and even give multiple translations. I'll evaluate to whatever languages are currently selected, if there's a matching language.
If you want to make me with some other values, you can do this:
\"Here are some sums \1 + 2\, \2 + 3\, \3 + 4\"\
See how elegantly I just evaluated those sums, and placed them inside the @Text?
I have one last little secret: did you know we all have a unique number? It's true! You can refer to us by writing @U/ and our number. For example, @FunctionDefinition is 192:
See how @U/192 turned into @FunctionDefinition? I hear you call these numbers 'Unicode'.
Otherwise, there just so many glorious functions that @FunctionDefinition made for me to do all kinds of things with words!

doc: I evaluate to the number of legible characters in the text; one letter is one character, one emoji is one character, etc. For example:

notequals.doc: \⊤\ if I am /not/ the same character sequence as the given @Text.

\'hello verse!'.starts('hello')\
\'hello verse!'.starts('verse')\

\'I am not a question.'.ends('?')\

doc: I make a new @Text that's me, with every letter in uppercase:
\'hello'.uppercase()\
Letters only have cases in some writing systems, so text in a writing system without them, like Japanese or Arabic, is unchanged.
My language tag decides whose rules to use. Turkish has a dotted and a dotless i, and only text tagged as Turkish uppercases them the Turkish way:
\'iyi'/tr.uppercase()\
\'iyi'.uppercase()\
I make a new @Text that's me, with every letter in lowercase:
\'HELLO'.lowercase()\
Make two texts lowercase to compare them without caring about capitalization. This keeps every word that starts with an a, whether or not it's capitalized:
\['Apple' 'apricot' 'Banana'].filter(ƒ(word•'') word.lowercase().starts('a'))\
Like @Text/uppercase, letters only have cases in some writing systems, and my language tag decides whose rules to use.
I make a new @Text from a piece of me. Counting starts at 1, and both ends are included:
\'hello'.subsequence(2 4)\
Leave the end out and I go all the way to my last symbol:
\'hello'.subsequence(3)\
I count symbols the way you see them, so an emoji made of several parts is still one symbol and never gets cut in half:
\'🐈📚!'.subsequence(1 2)\
If you ask for more than I have, I give you what I have.

inputs.doc: The place to start, counting from 1.
The place to stop, counting from 1. Leave it out to go to the end.

doc: I tell you where the given @Text first shows up in me, counting from 1:
\'hello'.index('ll')\
If it isn't in me at all, I give @None instead:
\'hello'.index('z')\
Together with @Text/subsequence I can take everything up to something — here, the first word:

\phrase: 'hello world'
phrase.subsequence(1 (phrase.index(' ') ?? 1) - 1)\

inputs.doc: The @Text to look for in me.

doc: I make a new @Text with every occurence of one @Text swapped for another:
Every occurrence changes, not just the first:
\'ha ha ha'.replace('ha' 'ho')\
If you ask me to replace an empty @Text, I give myself back unchanged.

inputs.doc: The @Text to look for in me.
The @Text to put in its place.

doc: I make a new @Text with the blank space taken off both of my ends. Space in the middle stays:

This is handy for text someone typed, which often carries extra spaces you didn't ask for.
I make a new @Text with my symbols in the opposite order:
\'hello'.reverse()\
I reverse the order of my symbols the way you see them, so emoji stay whole and letters keep their accents:
\'🐈📚'.reverse()\
I make a new @Text that's me, repeated the number of times of \count\:
If you give me a fractional @Number, I ignore the fraction:
If you give me a negative @Number or zero, I give an empty @Text.
The longest text I can make is 65,535 characters. If you try to make a longer text, I'll repeat the text as many times as I can.

doc: I'm a sequence of values, of any kind!
You can put anything in me: @Boolean, @Number, @Text, @None, even other @List, @Set, @Map, or any @expression. Here's a simple one:
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango']\
What makes me special is that I keep things in order and I number everything from 1 to however many items are in me.
My items are numbered, starting from 1. You can get values that I'm storing with @ListAccess, using their number:
For example, the second @value in this list is \['banana']\
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango'][2]\
I can have anything in me. Look at this list, with @Text, @Number, and @Time!
\['apple' 10 + 10 Time()]\

When you give me a list of many things, I'll generalize them if they have a @type in common. But sometimes you might literally mean those specific things. If you do, just put a ! after me, and I'll make sure that I represent a list of specifically only those values.
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango']!\
That's kind of it. But I can do all kinds of exciting things with my @FunctionDefinition!

doc: It creates a different number every time you evaluate it.
This creates a wonderful chaos that comes with unpredictability.
By default, it gives @Number values between \0\ and \1\:
\Random()\
But you can give it a @value, and it will generate values between \0\ and the value:
\Random(10)\
And if you give it two values, it will generate values between and including the two values:
\Random(-10 10)\
If your ranges have units, they will be preserved (and if they don't match, the minimum's unit will be used):
\Random(-10m 10m)\
And if you give numbers with particular numbers of significant digits after the decimal point, that precision will be preserved.

inputs.doc: The minimum @value that will be created, or if it's larger than 0, the maximum value. If @None is provided, then the minimum is \0\.
The maximum @value that will created, or if its smaller than the minimum provided, the minimum. If @None is provided, then the maximum is \1\.

doc: It's a stream of the names your audience selects by clicking, tapping, or pressing /Enter/ on a named @Phrase.
/clickety tap!/
So the best way to use it is to create a performance with named selectable phrases @Phrase, and then use a @Reaction to decide what to do when that name is chosen.
Here's the simplest example:

\Group(
Stack() 
[
Phrase('one' selectable:⊤ name:'1') 
Phrase('two' selectable:⊤ name:'2') 
Phrase(Choice())
]
)\
Copy this into the editor and then select one of the two @Phrase. You'll see the third @Phrase shows the name that was selected.
It tells you whether the mouse or trackpad's primary button is pressed, as a stream of @Boolean.
/click click click/
Of course, a mouse or trackpad isn't an ideal choice for listening to an audience, since not everyone can use one. The more accessible choice is @Choice.
But if you /really/ need to listen to a mouse button, this is the way to do it. It will provide a stream of @Boolean, representing whether the primary button is up \⊥\ or down \⊤\.
Here's a simple example:
\Phrase(Button() → '')\
This just makes a @Phrase that is the @value of the stream as text. If you copy it into the editor and click, you'll see it toggle back and forth between \⊥\ and \⊤\.

down.doc: If @None, the stream will provide both up and down values. If a \⊤\, it will only change with the button is pressed. If given a \⊥\, it will only change when the button is released.

doc: It tracks where your audience is pointing on @Stage.
/whrrrrrr/
Of course, this is not an accessible choice: not everyone can see or easily point, so be really sure you're not excluding someone from participating by using this stream.
If you're sure no one is excluded, then using @Pointer is as simple as just making a stream:
\Pointer()\
The @Place it provides will correspond to where on @Stage the pointer is pointing.
It tells you which keyboard @key your audience is pressing and releasing.
/clickety/
Try this
\Key()\
See how when you type a key, it shows up on @Stage? Every time a key is pressed down, a new @Text is added to the stream, describing the key that was pressed.
For a key that represents a character, the @value will be the character as @Text.

For special keys, like the /Escape/ key, it will be @Text that describes the key, using a <pre-defined name@https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/UI_Events/Keyboard_event_key_values>, unfortunately available only in English.
If you only want to know about a particular key, you can provide it:
\Key('a')\
And if you only want to know when when a @Key is released instead of pressed, you can provide a @Boolean:

key.doc: If @None, than all keys are provided. If a specific @Text, then only that key is provided.

down.doc: IF @None, then @key down generates inputs. If \⊤\, then only down inputs are provided, and if \⊥\, then only release inputs are provided.

doc: It ticks forward at a frequency you choose.
/tick tick tick/
Each time it does, @Program reevaluates with the new time @value.
For example:
\Time()\
If you provide time a @Time.frequency, it will tick at that rate. For example:
\Time(1000ms)\
However, there are limits to how small it can be, since @Program needs time to evaluate before they can respond to the next tick.
The smallest is probably around \20ms\.

frequency.doc: This is the frequency with which time should tick. It defaults to \33ms\, which is about 30 times per second.

relative.doc: If \⊤\, time starts at 0, when the program is first evaluated. Otherwise, it starts at the number of milliseconds since the start of today, UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), allowing you to keep track of the time of day.

doc: I tick a new @Moment at whatever pace you choose, so a program always knows today's date and the current time.
This makes a localized clock one line of code:
\Phrase(Now() → '')\
By default I tick every second. Give me a @Now.frequency in seconds, minutes, or hours to change the pace:
\Now(1min)\
My @Now.timezone and @Now.calendar mirror @Moment's inputs, and configure the Moments I create. For example, here's a clock showing the current time in Tokyo, on the Japanese calendar:
\Now(1s 'Asia/Tokyo' 'japanese')\
If those inputs change — say, a reaction gives me a different time zone — I start making Moments with the new settings.

How am I different from @Time? @Time counts the milliseconds since a program started, which is good for animation. I tell you the wall-clock date and time in a calendar and time zone, which is good for clocks and calendars.

frequency.doc: How often I make a new @Moment, in seconds, minutes, or hours. If \ø\, I tick every \1s\.

timezone.doc: A standard time zone name for the Moments I make, made of a region and a city, like \'America/New_York'\ or \'Asia/Tokyo'\. Don't know the name? Write a city you know and I'll suggest the closest time zone. If \ø\, I use the time zone of the device the program is running on.

calendar.doc: A Unicode calendar name for the Moments I make, like \'gregory'\, \'hebrew'\, \'chinese'\, or \'japanese'\. If \ø\, I use the calendar of the reader's locale.

doc: I am a single moment in time: a date on a calendar, a time of day, and the time zone and calendar they are expressed in.
All of my properties are optional. Give me date parts to describe a date:
Or just time parts, for a time of day:
\Moment(hour: 15 minute: 30) → ''\

If you give me no parts at all, I convert as the current date and time, wherever the program is running. If you leave out parts, any part bigger than the biggest one you gave comes from the current date and time, and smaller parts start at their beginning: so \Moment(month: 12) → ''\ is December 1 of this year, at midnight. Converting me only shows the kinds of parts you gave: date parts make a date, time parts make a time, and both make both:
\Moment() → ''\

My @Moment.timezone takes a standard IANA time zone name like \'America/Los_Angeles'\ or \'Asia/Tokyo'\; if you leave it \ø\, I use the time zone of the device the program is running on. My @Moment.calendar takes a Unicode calendar name like \'gregory'\, \'hebrew'\, or \'japanese'\; if you leave it \ø\, I use the calendar of the reader's locale. My @Moment.year, @Moment.month, and @Moment.day are in that calendar:
\Moment(5786 10 4 calendar: 'hebrew') → ''\
Converting me to @Text formats me for the reader's locale: the same Moment renders differently in English, 中文, or हिन्दी, and changes when the reader's locale changes.
My @Moment.era, @Moment.week, and @Moment.weekday are informational: @Now fills them in when it makes Moments, but they are ignored when formatting.
If you want a stream of Moments that updates as time passes — a clock — see @Now. If you want the milliseconds elapsed since your program started — for animation — see @Time.

year.doc: The year, in my calendar. For example, the Gregorian year \2026\ is the Hebrew year \5786\.

month.doc: The month of the year in my calendar, starting at \1\.

hour.doc: The hour of the day, from \0\ to \23\.

timezone.doc: A standard time zone name, made of a region and a city, like \'America/New_York'\, \'Europe/Paris'\, or \'Asia/Tokyo'\. Don't know the name? Write a city you know and I'll suggest the closest time zone. If \ø\, I use the time zone of the device the program is running on.

calendar.doc: A Unicode calendar name, like \'gregory'\, \'hebrew'\, \'chinese'\, or \'japanese'\. If \ø\, the calendar of the reader's locale.

era.doc: The era my year is in, like \'ce'\ or \'reiwa'\. Informational: @Now sets it, and formatting ignores it.

week.doc: The week of the year, starting at \1\. Informational: @Now sets it, and formatting ignores it.

weekday.doc: The day of the week, from \1\ (Monday) through \7\ (Sunday). Informational: @Now sets it, and formatting ignores it.

conversion.text: A @Text version of me, formatted for the reader's locale, in my calendar and time zone. Add a language after the @Text type to format for a specific locale, like \Moment(2026 7 1) → ''/es\.

error.timezone: this is not a valid time zone name
error.calendar: this is not a supported calendar name

doc: It's a stream of the microphone's loudness, from 0 to 1.
/bzzzzzzz/
It's sampled at the frequency of your choice. By default, the frequency is \30hz\, or 30 times per second, but you can change it to anything less frequent.
\Volume()\
This is great for listening to how loud the audience is!
It's a stream of the microphone's pitch, in hertz.
/hummmmm/
It's sampled at the frequency of your choice. The human voice is between 20Hz and 5000Hz, so plan on numbers in that range.
\Pitch()\
This is great for listening the tone that someone is speaking or singing.
It recognizes speech and turns it into @Text.
/hello there!/
It uses your browser's speech recognition to listen to what you say and turn it into words (isn't this so cool?!).
\Speech()\
This is perfect for those who can speak a @language but are still learning to read or write it (and more)...
You can specify a language code to recognize speech in a particular language:
\Speech(language: 'es-MX')\
If no language is specified, it defaults to your preferred language.
Speech recognition requires microphone access and Internet connection (please give access!). Also, there might be usage limits, so don't leave it on for too long (nooooo)!

reset.doc: When this @value changes, clear the accumulated speech and start fresh.

language.doc: A BCP 47 @language code (e.g., 'en-US'). If it's not supported by your browser's speech recognition, you'll get an error. It defaults to your preferred language.

limit.doc: The maximum number of words to keep in the accumulated speech (sliding window). When set, only the most recent words are kept, and older words are discarded. If not specified, all words are kept indefinitely.

error.browserNotSupported: service not supported in this browser

doc: It gives you a @List of @Color from your camera, one per frame.
/bzzzzzzz/
That @List essentially represents an image, but it's up to you to decide what to do with it.
You could try to represent the image with a bunch of @Phrase, which could look pretty cool! Try copying this...
But you could also analyze the colors to decide if a light was on or off, or if a particular color was common, letting the audience influence a performance with the colors they show.

width.doc: The number of @Color to sample in a row.

height.doc: The number of @Color to sample in a @column.

doc: It tracks a hand seen by your camera — where it is, which fingers are up, and which way it faces.
/wiggle wiggle/
Hold your hand up, wave it around, count on your fingers — @Hand follows.

Behind the scenes, @Hand uses a machine-learning model. The first time you use it in a program the model takes a few seconds to download, and a tiny spinning hand appears in the top-right corner of the stage while it loads. After that it stays cached and starts instantly.
Each frame, @Hand gives you a @Gesture — look there for the full list of inputs and what they mean.
Try this — it shows an emoji that matches your hand pose wherever your real hand is:

\hand: Hand()
Phrase((hand.open ? '🖐️' '✊') place: hand.place)\

resolution.doc: The width in pixels at which to sample the camera before running the hand model. Higher values can give slightly more accurate landmarks but cost more time per frame.

doc: It tracks a face seen by your camera — where it is, and what it's doing: open or closed eyes, an open mouth, a smile, a frown, raised eyebrows, and which way the head is turned.
/say cheese/
Look at the camera, smile, wink, open wide — @Face follows along.

Behind the scenes, @Face uses a machine-learning model. The first time you use it in a program the model takes a few seconds to download, and a tiny spinning face appears in the top-right corner of the stage while it loads. After that it stays cached and starts instantly.
Each frame, @Face gives you an @Expression. Look there for the full list of inputs and what they mean.
This example shows an emoji that matches your face wherever your real face is:

\face: Face()
Phrase((face.smiling ? '😀' face.mouthOpen ? '😮' '😐') place: face.place)\

resolution.doc: The width in pixels at which to sample the camera before running the face model. Higher values can give slightly more accurate landmarks but cost more time per frame.

doc: It tells you what things your camera sees — a cat, a cup, a book — and where they are.
/what's that/
Hold something up to the camera and @Objects will try to name it.
Behind the scenes, @Objects uses a machine-learning model that knows 80 kinds of everyday things.
Each frame, @Objects gives you a @List of @Thing, sorted by how sure the model is, with the surest first. Look at @Thing for what each one tells you.
The model is only guessing, so it will sometimes be wrong, or see nothing at all. Ask for a higher `confidence` to hear only the guesses it's surest about.
Here's an example that labels everything the camera sees:
\Stage(Objects() ↦ Phrase(⬚.name place: ⬚.place))\
You can also look for just one kind of thing, and ignore the rest:

\things: Objects(category: 'cat')
Phrase(things.length() > 0 ? '🐈' '…')\

inputs.doc: The time between samples.
The width in pixels at which to sample the camera before looking for things. The model looks at a 320 pixel square, so larger values mostly cost time.
An optional kind of thing to look for, ignoring everything else.
How sure the model has to be before I mention a thing, from 0 to 1. Higher means fewer but better guesses.
The most things to mention at once.

doc: It shows a @List of @Phrase or @Group one at a time, stopping on the last.
/Boop boop boop/

To control timing, you can either set the @Phrase.duration on each output, and it will show it for that long before moving on to the next one, and use whatever @Phrase.entering or @Phrase.exiting transitions you might have set. If you set them to a @Sequence, it will use the its duration.
All of that lets you do things like this little @Scene, which shows these three phrases in sequence:

\Scene([
	Phrase('Hello' duration: 1s)
	Phrase('How are you?' duration: 2s rotation: 5° entering: Pose(rotation: 0°))
	Phrase('I am fine')
])\
See how the first output is shown for a second, then the next for two seconds, but animated to a five degree rotation, and then it shows the last one?
You can make very elaborate sequences of output and animations with @Scene, and even make portions of them dynamic or interactive, as with any other @Phrase or @Group.
If you have animated output that is nested (a @Group with animated @Phrase inside), @Scene will wait for all of the animated content in the @Group to finish.
Oh, and one last little secret! You can even put @Boolean in the list, and if they are \⊥\, the @Scene will pause and wait for it to become true.
For example, if you wanted to make a sequence of @Phrase and only advance when @Button changes, you could do this:

\click: ∆ Button()
Scene([
	Phrase('Hello')
	click
	Phrase('How are you?' duration: 0.25s rotation: 5° entering: Pose(rotation: 0°))
	click
	Phrase('I am fine')
])\
See how it pauses after each @Phrase, and waits for @Button to change before advancing?

outputs.doc: The list of outputs to show in sequence.

doc: It moves a starting @Phrase with gravity and physics.
/boing boing boing/
You give it a starting @Phrase, and then it refines it with a new place and rotation based on gravity.
This lets you do really simple things like creating bouncing emoji:
\Motion(Phrase('o') startplace: Place(0m 10m))\🪲
See how the o bounces? On the first evaluation, you give it a place up high on @Stage, but then after, it gets @None, which allows @Motion to change it to whatever position gravity would place it.
Check out the many other ways to configure it below.
It's a stream of the @Text messages your audience types.
For example, this simple program checks if the message is 'hello', and if it is, the program evaluates to 'hi'. Otherwise, it evaluates to 'huh'?
\Chat().has('hello') ? 'hi!' 'huh?'\
That's it! You can make all kinds of performances with this, like chat bots, text adventures, or text-based control schemes for other kinds of performances.
It traces the outline of each letter's glyph as a @List of @Place.
Give it some text and a font face, and it'll trace each glyph's outline point by point.
\Contour('a' "Noto Sans")\
Feed those @Place values to a @List of @Phrase to see the outline drawn as dots:
\Stage(Contour('a' "Noto Sans" 10m).translate(ƒ(point) Phrase('•' place: point)))\

You can scale the outline with a @Number of meters, move its origin with a @Place, choose a font weight, turn on italics, and set the `spacing` between points as a distance in meters. A smaller `spacing` traces the outline more closely, with evenly spaced points along both lines and curves.
Some glyphs, like color emoji, have no outline, so they add no points. While it fetches the font, it'll give you an empty @List, then fill it in when it's ready.

inputs.doc: The text whose glyph outlines I should trace.
The font face to trace the glyphs in.
The height of the glyph in meters, scaling the outline.
An optional origin @Place to offset every point by.
The font weight to use, snapped to the nearest the face supports.
Whether to use the italic version of the face, if it has one.
The distance in meters between sampled points along the outline, kept consistent along lines and curves alike. Smaller values trace more finely, down to a minimum of 0.01 meters.
The order of the points: 'forward' or 'backward'.

error.connection: I couldn't reach the internet to get the font, so I can't trace its letters.
error.unavailable: I couldn't find that font's file, so I can't trace its letters.
error.unreadable: I downloaded the font, but I couldn't read it, so I can't trace its letters.
error.outline: I loaded the font, but I couldn't get the shape of these letters.

doc: It lets your audience drag @Output to a @Place on @Stage.
There are many ways to place @Output on @Stage: give them an explicit @Place, use @Motion and let gravity do its work, or put them in a @Group to be arranged.
But sometimes you want to give the /audience/ control over where @Output goes on @Stage.
Here's how it works: make a @Placement and give it to an @Output's @Place:
\Phrase('hi' place: Placement())\
Then, any time the audience uses an arrow @key or clicks or taps on stage, the @Placement will make a new @Place that moves in the desired direction.
Try copying this to your program and moving the @Output with the pointer or keyboard.
You can customize the @Placement, enabling and disabling movement on certain dimensions, changing how far a @Place moves, and the initial @Place the stream starts with.

inputs.doc: The initial place to start with.
How many meters the place should move when the audience requests a move.
If true, allows movement on the horizontal axis. On by default.
If true, allows movement on the vertical axis. On by default.
If true, allows movement on the z-axis, with the + and - keys.

doc: It fetches the text at a web address you give it.
The internet is fascinating — a whole world of connected computers sharing documents with each other.
This stream connects to it — give it a URL, like this:
\Webpage('https://wordplay.dev')\

And there's apparently this thing called <CSS@https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/CSS/First_steps/What_is_CSS>, which lets you @query things on a web page? Give it a CSS selection query and it'll get only the text that matches that query. Like this example, which gets the level one headers.
\Webpage('https://wordplay.dev' 'h1')\

Lots of things can go wrong with this one. If you lose your internet connection, or the URL doesn't resolve to anything, or the URL isn't public, or the URL isn't an HTML page… All of these can lead to exception. If if you find a page that works, you'll get some @Number indicating a percent complete and then a @List of the words on the page.

url.doc: The HTML webpage URL to get.

query.doc: The CSS @query to evaluate on the HTML

frequency.doc: The number of minutes that should pass before the page is fetched again.

error.invalid: this is not a valid URL
error.limit: too many requests to this domain

doc: It's a stream of @Rebound values for when named @Output bump into each other.

To have two @Output notice each other, give them both names, then give me both names. I'll make a new @Rebound whenever they touch. They don't need @Matter for that — a name is all I need to watch something.

Give me one name instead, and I'll tell you whenever that @Output touches anything else in the physical world. An @Output is in the physical world if it has @Matter, if a @Motion places it, if it's a @Shape directly on the @Stage, or if I'm watching its name too.

Noticing isn't the same as bouncing. @Output only pushes other @Output around if it has @Matter and a @Motion moving it. @Output that your program places goes exactly where you put it, so it passes through whatever it touches — I'll still tell you about the touch.
A @Rebound has the names that touched and the direction they touched from. Right after I make one, I'll make a \ø\, since a collision is over as soon as it happens.
I can only watch @Output placed directly on the @Stage. Anything inside a @Group moves in that group's own space, so I can't see it — give the @Group a name and watch that instead.

subject.doc: The name of the @Output I should watch. Watching it is enough to put it in the physical world, so it doesn't need @Matter.

object.doc: The name of the other @Output I should watch. With this given too, I only report those two touching; leave it out and I report the first one touching anything in the physical world.

doc: I give a new @value every time playing @Music reaches a beat, so you can build visuals that move with the music. I always have a @Downbeat for you, so you can read it straight away: before any music plays I sit on beat zero with nothing sounding, and my \tempo\ stays zero until it starts.
